sections.h2: Who bills property tax in the city of Champaign
sections.html:
The city of Champaign sends no property tax bill of its own. The Champaign County Treasurer, who also acts as Collector, bills every parcel inside the city, along with the school districts and other taxing districts that overlap it. Valuation belongs to the Champaign County Supervisor of Assessments. The city lines up with Champaign City township, so a single township assessor covers the whole municipality.

For a seller this is simple. One PIN identifies the parcel, and the same two county offices answer your questions whether the house is near Campustown, downtown or on the northwest side by Parkland College.

Champaign is a city of about 23 square miles in central Illinois. The mid-2025 estimate is 91,195 residents, and owners live in 43.8% of homes, so renters are the majority. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $210,900, and median gross rent is $1,123. The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign on the east side and Parkland College on the northwest give the market a large student population during the school year.

A landlord selling a rental near campus will often be dealing with tenants and a lease cycle, and the tax bill follows the parcel no matter who lives in it. Older houses, especially those built in the 1980s or earlier, draw close looks at the roof and heating system, so check both before you list.

Several districts pull demand in different directions:

  • Downtown Champaign: the historic core with newer mixed-use buildings and a parking deck.
  • Campustown: the Green Street district beside the university, where high-rise student apartments have opened since 2008.
  • North Prospect: a shopping corridor on the city's northern edge.
  • Northwest and west sides: home to Parkland College and St. Thomas More High School.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
The bill is mailed by early May and falls due in two installments, normally in June and September. A payment postmarked on the due date is on time. Each coupon carries its own dates, so use the bill in front of you.

Late payments pick up interest of 1.5% a month, and the Treasurer accepts personal checks through September 30. A returned payment is void and costs $30 plus statutory interest. Pay by card or eCheck online or by phone at 217-834-8713, and expect a fee from the processing vendor. In person, the Treasurer's counter is at 102 E. Main Street in Urbana.

The Board of Review takes complaints from July 1 through September 10. Its hours are 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Thursday, or by appointment. Township assessors value a home as of January 1 at one-third of market value, and change notices from the Supervisor of Assessments reach owners before the complaint window opens.

Gather evidence that fits your property. For a house, that means your purchase price if you bought recently, a recent appraisal, and sales of similar homes in the same neighborhood. After September 10 the board reviews the complaints and issues written decisions.

Each reduction comes off equalized assessed value before the tax rate is applied.

For forms, call the Assessment Office at 217-384-3760. Faxed or emailed applications are refused. If you moved in recently, ask whether an earlier owner's exemption carried over before assuming it did.

The county sells unpaid tax to a buyer at its annual sale on October 30, for amounts still open after 4:30 p.m. on October 29. The house itself is not sold. After the sale you owe the amount sold plus interest, and you redeem through the County Clerk at 217-384-3722.

The Clerk sends a Take Notice within four months of the sale. Under 35 ILCS 200/21-350 the redemption period is generally 3 years from the sale date, with listed exceptions. If the owner does not redeem in time, the buyer may petition the circuit court for a deed.

sections.h2: Selling a Champaign house when tax is still due
sections.html:
Begin with the PIN. Ask the Treasurer which installments are paid, and ask the title company or attorney whether tax is owed for the year. Depending on the closing and recording dates, a bill may be addressed to the previous owner, who has to forward it to the new owner.

If installments are open, ask the title company how they will be handled at closing. Knowing the number early gives you room to choose a closing date. For a rental, put the tenants' lease end date on the same checklist.

A rough order of steps: pull the PIN, call the Treasurer at 217-384-3743 for the payment status, confirm what the title company will pay from your proceeds, and make sure the buyer's mailing address goes to the Treasurer so the next bill reaches the right person. Sellers who want to skip showings and repairs can ask whether a cash buyer will close around the open installment.

faqs.q: Does the city of Champaign collect its own property tax?
faqs.a: No. The Champaign County Treasurer bills and collects all property tax for parcels in the city, then distributes it to the taxing districts.

faqs.q: When is Champaign property tax due?
faqs.a: Bills are mailed by early May and are typically due in June and September. A payment postmarked on the due date counts as on time.

faqs.q: When can I file an assessment complaint for a Champaign home?
faqs.a: Between July 1 and September 10, with the Champaign County Board of Review, which is open 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Thursday.

faqs.q: What is the senior exemption in Champaign?
faqs.a: A $5,000 reduction in equalized assessed value for owners who reach 65 by the end of the assessment year. A separate freeze applies up to a $75,000 household income.

faqs.q: Do owners or renters make up most of Champaign?
faqs.a: Renters. Owners live in 43.8% of the city's homes.
